units.spoken: Model-Based RL: Dyna, AlphaZero, MuZero, World Models and Dreamer
Learn how the world responds, then plan or practice inside that model.

Take a look at this figure. Real steps teach the model, and planning inside the model improves the policy that acts. The methods split two ways: AlphaZero and MuZero look ahead with a search, while Dyna, World Models and Dreamer practise inside the model. That loop is the whole page: learn the world, then plan or practise inside what you learned.

Figure 1 shows the loop every model-based method on this page runs: real steps teach the model, and planning inside the model improves the policy that acts. The dashed box sorts the methods: AlphaZero and MuZero look ahead with a search, while Dyna, World Models and Dreamer practise inside the model. Take Dyna in a grid maze, where the agent starts on one square and must reach a goal square: one real step into the goal teaches the model, and replays inside it spread the value back without another real step.

A model-based agent learns, or is given, a model of the world. It plans or practices inside that model, and acts in the real world to collect steps that improve the model, the policy or both (Figure 1). The methods in RL Method Families, Policy Gradients: REINFORCE, Actor-Critic and PPO and Continuous-Action Actor-Critic: TD3 and SAC learn from real steps only; they are model-free.
Section one, Dyna
A chess player tries moves in their head before touching a piece; a model lets an agent do the same before spending real steps.

A model predicts the next state and reward from a state and a move; planning uses it to look ahead or practice without the real world. Dyna runs the Q-learning update from Q-Learning on imagined steps as well as real ones.
A real step into the goal teaches one square; the model lets the agent replay the square before it without moving (Figure 2).

Take a look at this figure. One real step into the goal lifts the score of the square next to it, and one imagined replay lifts the square one further back. The two arrows are the two kinds of step: the real one and the replay. That is the whole trick: value spreads backward from the goal one square per replay, without another real step.

Figure 2 shows one real step and one imagined replay side by side in the maze. The solid arrow is the real step into the goal, which lifts the score of the square next to it, and the dashed arrow is the replay, which lifts the square one further back. Take the square next to the goal: after the real step its score rises a little, and a replay then carries a smaller rise one square further back.
Dyna plans with a learned model, but the step that actually changes a score is the Q-learning update. Here is that update, with the model supplying extra steps to apply it to.
Take a look at this equation. The target is the reward plus the best score ahead, and the score moves part of the way toward it.

The target line. Target is the value the score should move toward. R is the reward the step earned. Gamma is the discount, so a reward one step later counts a little less. Max takes the best score over every move in the next state, Q of s prime and a prime, the highest value the agent can get from there. The plus adds the stored reward to the discounted future score. Intuitively, the target is the reward plus the best score waiting in the next square.
termList: max Q of s prime and a prime

units.spoken: Intuition. The score a square should aim at is the reward its step earns plus the best score waiting in the next square.
Example. Take the square next to the goal: a real step into the goal pays, so its target is that reward alone, with no best score added from the goal square, since the episode ends there.

The update line. Q of s and a is the score of action a in state s, the future reward expected from that move. The arrow reads replace with: the score on the left is replaced by the value on the right. The right side starts from the score as it stands now, and the second half adds the correction. Intuitively, start from the score as it stands, then correct it.
Intuition. A score is not set in one jump; the update starts from the score as it stands and corrects it.
Example. Take the square next to the goal after one real step: its score starts where it stood and moves only part of the way toward its target.

The correction row. Alpha, the learning rate, scales the gap, so the score moves only part of the way toward the target. The brackets hold the gap between target and the score as it stands, the one-step surprise: positive when the move turned out better than the score said, negative when worse, zero when the score was exactly right. The plus adds the scaled gap onto the current score. Intuitively, the correction is the surprise, scaled by the learning rate.
Intuition. The correction is the surprise: how far the target sits from the score as it stands.
Example. Take a replay where the target sits above the score: the gap is positive, so the score rises by a learning-rate share of it.
So the update aims at the target the step earned plus the discounted best score ahead, then moves the score part of the way there.

Take the square next to the goal. A real step into the goal gives that square a small value, and a replay then carries a smaller value one square further back, so value spreads backward from the goal one square per replay (Figure 2).

Dyna-Q adds n imagined steps from a remembered model after each real one. The code runs Dyna-Q on the 6 by 9 maze, one episode of steps. Env step of s and a is the maze's rule, returning r and s next.

This code runs Dyna-Q on the maze: it sets up the Q-table and an empty model, then repeats one real step plus n imagined replays until the goal is reached. Each real step learns from the maze and stores the step; each imagined step replays a stored step picked at random.
1. Sets the maze values, the Q-table, an empty model and the start and goal squares: alpha 0.1, gamma 0.95 and eps 0.1 are the Example 8.1 values, and n 5 is one of three counts tried: 0, 5 and 50.
2. The Q-learning update, line 2 of the Q-learning card above, with no future past the goal.
3. Picks a move epsilon-greedily, the best-scoring move (ties at random) except for a small chance epsilon of a random one, and takes one real step.
4. Learns from the real step and stores it in the model.
5. Replays n imagined steps, each a stored step picked at random (it picks a seen state, then a move tried there); n is the count that varies in Figure 3.
6. Runs one episode: start at the start square and call dyna step until the goal is reached.

Each imagined step can carry value, a square's best Q, one square further back from the goal, so the reward found there spreads through the maze without new real steps (the RL textbook, Example 8.1). Where a square has no value yet, all four moves there score 0 and the agent picks one at random; once value reaches the start, following the best move from each square gives a route to the goal. Reaching the goal ends an episode, and the agent starts again from the start.

Until the goal is first found every value is 0, so imagined steps change nothing and every n takes the same real steps to find it, on average. After that, a larger n forms the route in fewer real steps, at the cost of one update per imagined step, and with no imagined steps it is plain Q-learning, where each real step updates only the square it left. One random run can occasionally flip that order.

Take a look at this figure. The grid shows the maze with each square shaded by its score and arrows for the best move, and the bars show when a route forms for each setting of imagined steps. More imagined steps per real step form the route in fewer real steps: at a lot of imagined steps a route formed by step 72, while at several the readout still says no route yet at 150 real steps. The lesson is the trade: imagined steps buy real steps, at the cost of one update each.

Try it: the first slider sets the imagined steps per real step, and the second sets the real steps counted after finding the goal. Watch the grid shade by score and the bars mark when a route forms for each setting.

Figure 3 shows how imagined steps trade against real steps on the maze. The sliders set the imagined steps per real step and the real steps counted after finding the goal; the grid shades each square by its score with arrows for the best move, and the bars show when a route forms for each setting. Take several imagined steps at 150 real steps: the readout says no route yet, while at a lot it says a route formed by step 72.
Imagined steps matter most when real steps are slow or costly, as for a robot. Deep Q-Network (DQN)'s experience replay reuses stored real steps the same way, with a network in place of the table.
Section two, AlphaZero and MuZero

AlphaZero is a program that learns to play a board game well by playing games against itself, starting from nothing but the game's rules. It looks ahead with a tree search, a look-ahead over move sequences that a network steers, and the games teach the network.
Go is a board game where two players place stones on a grid to surround territory. In one Go position the network's first guesses are rough; search visits sharpen them (Figure 4).

Take a look at this figure. The network's chances and the search's chances sit side by side for three moves. Move 1 towers in the search's bars while move 3 stays short in both, and the scale puts the real result at plus one. The lesson: search visits sharpen rough first guesses into chances worth trusting.

Figure 4 shows the search sharpening the network's guesses on three moves. The orange bars are the network's chances and the teal bars are the search's, so move 1 towers in teal while move 3 stays short in both, and the scale at right puts the real result at plus one. Take move 1: the search trusts it far more than the network did, so the loss pulls the network's chance up toward the search's.
AlphaZero learns from games against itself.
Take a look at this equation. One look at a position gives the move chances and the predicted result, the search turns visits into trust, and the loss pulls the network toward both.

The first line. P is a probability for each move, and V is the predicted result. One call to the network F on a position S returns two things at once, a pair in brackets: P and V, the guesses in Figure 4. The equals sign says the pair on the left is what F gives for the position on the right. Intuitively, one look at a position gives both what to try and what to expect.
Intuition. One look at a position gives both what to try and what to expect.
Example. Take one Go position: the network gives a chance for every legal move and one predicted result, and the search starts from those guesses.

The second line. Pi of A is the chance the search gives move A. N of A counts how often the search tried move A from the current position, and Pi is those counts scaled to probabilities: each count divided by the total count over all moves, so the chances add to one. The sign reads in proportion to. The most visited move gets the highest chance, the least visited the lowest. Intuitively, the search's own count of visits becomes the move it trusts most.

Intuition. The search's own count of visits becomes the move it trusts most. The paper raises the counts to 1 over a temperature, a knob that spreads the chances out when high and sharpens them when low; here it is 1, so the counts stand as they are.
Example. Take a Go position where the search tried one move far more than the rest: that move takes most of the chance, and the game plays it.

The loss line. Loss is the training error, in two parts: a value part and a move part. Z is the game's final result, minus one for a loss, zero for a draw, plus one for a win. The first part squares the gap between the real result and V, so a far guess costs much more. The second part adds over moves the search's chance Pi times the network's log chance log P; the minus makes it positive, since log P is negative, and it is smallest when P matches Pi. Intuitively, training pulls the network's guesses toward the search's sharper ones and the game's true result.
Intuition. Training pulls the network's guesses toward the search's sharper ones and the game's true result.

Example. Take one Go position where the network's first guesses are rough: the search visits the most promising move most often, so its chances come out sharper, and the loss pulls the network toward them. The paper adds a small weight penalty term, which this card leaves out.
So the whole equation says this: match the search and the game.
Beyond the move chances, the loss also pulls the network's value guess toward the game's result.

MuZero is AlphaZero for games whose rules it is not given. Where AlphaZero is handed the rules and simulates them exactly, MuZero must learn the model too: it predicts what each move pays and where it leads, then searches inside that learned model (Figure 5).

Take a look at this figure. The board becomes the first hidden state, each move steps it forward with a predicted reward, and the network reads move chances and a value off each hidden state. The search runs on hidden states it imagines, never on pictures of the board. The lesson: the model is learned, not given, and the search still works.

Figure 5 shows MuZero's search running on hidden states, never on pictures of the board. The board becomes the first hidden state, each move steps it forward with a predicted reward, and the network reads move chances and a value off each hidden state. Take one move: dynamics predicts its reward and the next hidden state.
AlphaZero needed the rules of the game. MuZero learns the rules too, inside the network.
Take a look at this equation. A board becomes a hidden state, one imagined move pays and lands ahead, the same network judges hidden states, and the loss adds one error per step.

The first line. H sub zero is a hidden state, a list of numbers the network makes up, not a picture. The equals sign says H sub zero is what repr gives for the past observations, here the board. Intuitively, the board becomes a hidden state.
Intuition. A board becomes a short list of numbers the network invents for itself.
Example. Take one board: repr turns them into a hidden state, and every later step of the search reads that list, never the board.

The second line. R is the reward that move pays, and H sub k plus one is the next hidden state. One call to dynamics on H sub k and a move A returns both at once: R and H sub k plus one. The subscript K counts the steps played forward, so H sub k is the state at step K and H sub k plus one is the state one step on. The dynamics network stands in for the rules: it predicts the reward and the next state instead of the real game producing them. Intuitively, one imagined move pays a predicted reward and lands in a new hidden state.
Intuition. One imagined move pays a predicted reward and lands in a new hidden state.
Example. Take one hidden state and one move: dynamics predicts the reward that move pays and hands back the next hidden state, ready for the next imagined move.

The third line. P is a probability for each move, and V is the predicted result. The same network as the AlphaZero card's first line, read from a hidden state instead of a board: one call to F on H sub k returns P and V. The hidden state only has to predict rewards, moves and values, never to redraw the board. Intuitively, the same network that judged boards now judges hidden states.
Intuition. The same network that judged boards now judges hidden states.
Example. Take one hidden state halfway through the imagined steps: f reads it and gives move chances and a predicted result, just as it did from a board.

The loss line. Loss is the training error, added over the steps played forward. The sum over K adds one bracketed term per step, and each term is the three gaps added together. The first gap is L of U sub k and R sub k, the error between the reward really seen, U sub k, and the reward the dynamics predicted, R sub k. L is an error between a target and a prediction, squared error for reward and value in board games. Intuitively, training adds up one error per imagined step.
Intuition. Training adds up one error per imagined step, and each step's error has three parts.
Example. Take one step played forward where the model predicted no reward but the move paid: the first gap is the squared error between the seen reward and the predicted one.

The last row. The plus adds the second gap, L of Z sub k and V sub k, the error between the observed return and the guessed value, and the third gap, L of Pi sub k and P sub k, the cross-entropy between the search's and the network's chances. The cross-entropy counts, over moves, search chance times log of network chance, added up and flipped positive, smallest when the chances match. The sum pulls each predicted reward toward the reward seen, each value toward the observed return, and each P toward the search's Pi. Intuitively, learn the rules, the moves and the value together.
Intuition. The last two gaps teach the value guess and the move chances at each step.

Example. Take one step played forward where the search gave one move most of the chance: the third gap pulls the network's chances toward the search's at that step. The paper adds a small weight penalty term, which this card leaves out.
So the whole equation says this: learn the rules, the moves and the value together.

Take a stored stretch of play stepped through for a few moves. At each step played forward the model predicts the reward that move paid, the value of the position, and the chances the search gave the moves, and the loss pulls each prediction toward what really happened, so the learned rules get sharper with every stretch.
Section three, World Models and Dreamer

World Models learn a compact model of the game from what the agent sees, then train a small controller, the part that picks the moves, inside that model and run it for real. The controller can practice inside the model without touching the real game: real steps are slow and costly, imagined ones are cheap. In one game, VizDoom, a first-person shooter, it trained wholly inside the dream and then ran for real. Making the model's predictions more random kept the controller from exploiting the model's errors, since random predictions make the fake shortcuts in the model unreliable.

An agent that counts only the reward inside a fixed window of imagined steps becomes shortsighted. Dreamer fixes that by learning a compact hidden-state model from replayed experience and training its actor and critic on imagined runs inside it; the critic estimates the reward past the window, so the actor still aims for rewards that come later.
Dreamer's walker, a simulated walker rewarded for walking speed, practices inside its own model of the body, a few steps at a time (Figure 6).

Take a look at this figure. A walker imagines a few steps: the first two earn no reward and the third pays, each step's reward counting a little less than the one before, and the critic stands in for every reward past the window. Without the critic the return is much less. The lesson: the critic counts the rest, so a short imagined run still aims far ahead.

Figure 6 shows a short imagined run and what the critic adds to it. The first two steps earn no reward and the third pays, each step's reward counting a little less than the one before, and the red critic box stands in for every reward past the window.
The reward comes when it reaches walking speed; gamma is the discount, as in the return strip of RL Basics.
Dreamer trains its actor and critic on runs imagined inside the model, so it needs a return it can compute from imagined rewards alone.
Take a look at this equation. The return is the imagined rewards, each counting a little less, and the critic finishes what the window cuts off.

The return line. Return is the imagined return, the value of the walker's imagined run. The equals sign sets it to the rewards the model imagines for the walker: R sub zero is the reward at the first imagined step, and Gamma times R sub one is the reward at the second step times the discount Gamma, so a reward one step later counts a little less. The plus adds the two rewards together. Intuitively, the return starts with the first two imagined rewards.
Intuition. An imagined run is worth the rewards it earns, with later ones counting a little less.
Example. Take the walker's first imagined step: it earns no reward yet, so the return starts at zero and waits on the later steps.

The critic row. The dots mean the pattern keeps going: each later reward R sub k the walker earns is multiplied by Gamma to the K, the discount raised to one more power for every step further ahead, up to Gamma to the H minus one times R sub H minus one, the last reward inside the window of H steps. The final plus adds Gamma to the H times V of S sub H, the critic's guess for the walker's state at the end of the window, discounted H times: it stands in for every reward past the window, so the return is much more than it would be without the critic. Intuitively, the dots carry the same pattern forward, and the critic stands in for everything past the window.
Intuition. The dots carry the same pattern forward, and the critic stands in for everything past the window.
Example. Take the last imagined step: its reward counts the least, yet the return comes out much more than the rewards alone.
So the whole equation says this: the return, cut after H steps and finished by the critic.

Take the walker's imagined run inside the model. The first imagined steps earn nothing while the walker is still getting up to speed, then a later step pays when it reaches walking speed, so the actor learns from a short imagined run instead of a whole real one.
This return is one ingredient of Dreamer's lambda return, which blends short returns like this one, each weighted by a number called lambda, here 0.95.
Section four, Model-based methods in practice
What is known about the rules and what a real step costs decide the pick. The section Choosing a family sets these methods beside the model-free ones.

This table lines up the five methods side by side: when each fits, how often it learns or plans, what it carries, and what it costs. Read across a row to see how one method works, and down a column to see how the methods differ. Dyna-Q fits few states that fit in a table, rules unknown, real steps cost more than compute: one real update plus n imagined ones per real step, and it carries the Q-table and the stored model of seen steps, at a cost of n plus one updates per real step. AlphaZero fits rules known and exactly simulated, as in board games: more simulations look further ahead at more compute per move, and it carries the network and its stored self-play games, at a cost of many machines for self-play and few for training. MuZero fits rules unknown where look-ahead matters: playing further ahead trains the model to predict further ahead at more compute per sample, and it carries the three networks and a replay buffer of past games, at a cost of one learned-model step per imagined move. World Models fits rules unknown with pixels in, the idea Dreamer builds on: some random runs first, then the vision model compresses each frame, the memory model predicts the next compressed frame, then the controller learns by evolution, and it carries the vision, memory and controller models, at a cost of a small controller and a much larger vision model. Dreamer fits rules unknown with real steps costly: batches of replayed sequences, it imagines some steps ahead, a longer window counts more imagined reward before the critic takes over, and it carries the world model, actor, critic and a replay buffer, at a cost of no real steps for the actor and critic. The pattern: the more a method leans on the model, the less it leans on real steps, and the cost moves from real steps to compute.

Table 1 compares the five methods by when each fits and what it costs. Each row names one method, the setting it suits, how often it learns or plans, what it carries, and its cost, so the rows read as a choice between methods rather than a list of facts. Take Dreamer: where real steps are expensive, it learns from imagined runs without taking a real step.

Each method's code is public: AlphaZero (alpha-zero-general), MuZero (muzero-general), World Models (world-models) and Dreamer (dreamer, code from the Dreamer author). The Dyna-Q maze code is linked in Table 1.
4.1 When the model is wrong

The central failure of this family is a wrong model compounding its errors. The model is learned from limited play, so each imagined step is a little off, and the next imagined step starts from that wrong state, so the error grows with every step of the imagined run. The symptom is an agent that scores well inside its imagination and fails on the real task, chasing a route that works only in the model. The fix is to keep imagined runs short and few until the model has seen enough, and to keep checking the model against real steps: Dyna replays only steps it really saw (Stale and noisy models), and Dreamer imagines only a short stretch before its critic takes over (Model exploitation and short sight).

Two more failures come with the family. A stale model keeps replaying a world that has changed, so the agent never finds the shorter path a new opening allows; Dyna-Q-plus fixes it by re-checking moves not tried for a long time (Stale and noisy models). And search costs compute: more simulations look further ahead, but each move costs more, so the fix is to cap the search or the steps played forward and let the network carry what the search would have found (Thin searches and repeated games; Model drift, mixed scales and stale targets).

The methods in this series ran on small examples such as CartPole, a pole balanced on a moving cart, and a maze. What does it take to train one on a real agent, a banana collector, a game agent that sees 37 sensor numbers? Deep Q-Networks (DQN) builds that agent with replay, a target network, a second copy held still while the main one learns, and the Double and Dueling changes.
